source.title: Some Open Questions in Wave Chaos

accepted.question_text: For a compact unit-area Riemannian surface of negative curvature with quantum Hamiltonian P = sqrt(-Δ), eigenvalues λ_k, and counting function N(λ) = #{k: λ_k ≤ λ} = λ^2/(4π) + R(λ), can one prove that a generic negatively curved surface has Weyl remainder R(λ) = O(λ^ε) for every ε > 0? More broadly, which refined dynamical quantities of the geodesic flow determine the sharp high-energy spectral remainder beyond the known O(λ/log λ) bound?
accepted.context_brief: Generic Weyl remainder in negative curvature

evidence.quote: For any surface of unit area, the behaviour of the spectral counting function N(λ) = # {k ∈ N, λ k ≤ λ} is asymptotically given by the celebrated Weyl’s law (1) N(λ) = λ 2 / 4π + R(λ), with a remainder R(λ) = O(λ) when λ → ∞.
for a negatively curved surface, one can prove that R(λ) = O(λ/ logλ) [2]; one actually expect that, for a “generic” such surface, R(λ) = O(λ ǫ) for any ǫ> 0.
The topological pressure, the entropy, the Ruelle-Pollicott spectrum associated with the geodesic flow, should “naturally” arise in the description of the quantum spectrum.

accepted.question_text: For chaotic quantum systems, can the Gutzwiller trace formula and related semiclassical propagator approximations be justified for times substantially larger than the Ehrenfest time T_E ≈ log(λ)/χ_Lya, and in particular on time scales relevant for sharp spectral statistics? The problem asks how to control the quantum evolution after exponential separation of classical trajectories causes the usual semiclassical approximation to break down.
accepted.context_brief: Gutzwiller trace formula beyond Ehrenfest time

evidence.quote: The rule of the game is: the further in time you control the propagator, the more precise your spectral estimate becomes.

For a chaotic system, trajectories separate from each other at an exponential rate, which results in a breakdown of semiclassical approximations around the Ehrenfest time TE ≈ log λ / χ Lya, where χ Lya is the largest Lyapunov exponent.
In that view, a present line of investigation consists in trying to extend the validity of the Gutzwiller approximation to larger times [11].

accepted.question_text: Can the Bohigas-Giannoni-Schmit, or random matrix theory, conjecture be proved rigorously for generic chaotic quantum Hamiltonians, so that the local high-energy spectrum at the mean level spacing scale δλ ∼ 2π/λ has the same statistics as the appropriate Gaussian random matrix ensemble such as the Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble? A proof would need to justify the periodic-orbit expansion at times comparable to the Heisenberg time T_H ∼ λ and show that the sum over non-correlated pairs of periodic orbits is negligible relative to the correlated pairs.

evidence.quote: The BGS conjecture claims that, provided the classical dynamics is chaotic, this sequence is statistically equivalent with that formed by the eigenvalues of a random matrix belonging to one of the three standard Gaussian ensembles (in the present case the Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble, made of real-symmetric matrices with independent Gaussian entries).
Yet, this remarkable result is still far from achieving a rigorous proof of the BGS conjecture.
Firstly, the Gutzwiller approximation has been applied to times of order TH ≫ TE, for which its validity is only speculative.
The second problem seems more formidable: one needs to prove that the huge sum of “non-correlated pairs” is effectively negligible compared to that over correlated ones.

accepted.question_text: For arithmetic negatively curved surfaces, or analogous systems such as the quantum cat map, can one give a full rigorous proof that the two-point correlation function of the high-energy quantum spectrum converges to the correlation function of Poisson-distributed points rather than to random matrix statistics? The issue is to control the additional periodic-orbit correlations caused by large degeneracies of the length spectrum.
accepted.context_brief: Poisson statistics for arithmetic quantum chaos

evidence.quote: In the case of arithmetic surfaces (or the quantum cat map), the orbit lengths are highly degenerate (they are simple functions of integer numbers), so many more pairs of orbits are correlated than in the generic case.
The above approach implies that the 2-point function converges to that of Poisson-distributed points, quite different from RMT [6].
statistics has been checked numerically, but a full proof of is still lacking (mainly due to the “second problem” mentioned above) [25].

accepted.question_text: What refined dynamical property separates exceptional arithmetic chaotic systems from generic chaotic systems for purposes of spectral universality, and how generic is that property among all negatively curved surfaces? The candidate property should go beyond global chaoticity, should likely restrict large degeneracies and near-degeneracies in the length spectrum {ℓ_γ}, and may require a Diophantine condition on the differences ℓ_γ − ℓ_γ′.
accepted.context_brief: Dynamical criterion for generic spectral universality

evidence.quote: The existence of such “exceptional” surfaces invalidates any proof of the BGS conjecture which would be only based on global chaotic properties.
To prove the conjecture, one will need to exhibit a more refined dynamical property able to explicitly separate the exceptional systems from the generic ones.

The above results suggest that this property may concern the length spectrum: it should probably forbid large degeneracies length degeneracies, but must also deal with almost-degeneracies, maybe by requiring some diophantine condition on the differences {ℓγ − ℓγ′}.
Among all surfaces of negative curvature, how generic are those satisfying this property?

accepted.question_text: If the Laplace-Beltrami operator on an arithmetic surface is perturbed by generic selfadjoint lower-order terms, or if one changes the quantization scheme attached to the same classical geodesic flow, does the resulting quantum spectrum become universal in the random-matrix sense? If universality can be restored this way, how large must the lower-order perturbing terms be?

evidence.quote: a perturbation of the Laplacian by (selfadjoint) lower-order terms still makes up a “quantization” of the geodesic flow.
The problem of “genericity” then may as well concern the various quantizations attached to a given classical dynamics [36].

For instance, if one perturbs the Laplacian on an arithmetic surface by “generic” lower-order terms, does the resulting spectrum become universal? If yes, how large must be the perturbing terms to achieve “universality”?

accepted.question_text: For Laplacian eigenfunctions ψ_k on a negatively curved compact surface and their phase-space semiclassical measures μ_k, what is the rate and limiting distribution of the quantum averages μ_k(f) for a fixed phase-space observable f as λ_k grows? In particular, for a generic chaotic system, is the distribution Gaussian with variance asymptotic to Var(f)/λ, as predicted by Feingold and Peres, and can the current gap between the expected O(λ^−1) variance and the proven O(1/log λ) upper bound be closed?
accepted.context_brief: Rates and distributions in quantum ergodicity

evidence.quote: At which rate does this convergence take place? Namely, for a given phase space observable f, how fast does μ k(f) → μ L(f)?
One would actually like to understand the distribution of the elements {μ k(f), λ k ≤ λ} in the limit λ → ∞.

Feingold and Peres have conjectured that, for a generic chaotic system, the distribution should be Gaussian with variance ∼ Var(f)/λ, where Var(f) is the variance appearing in the classical Central Limit Theorem [13].
The gap between the expected O(λ −1) and the proved O(1/ logλ) is (once more) due to our present inability to control the quantum evolution beyond the Ehrenfest time TE ∼ logλ.

accepted.question_text: Can Quantum Unique Ergodicity be proved for non-arithmetic negatively curved surfaces and higher-dimensional negatively curved manifolds, meaning that every high-energy semiclassical measure μ_k of Laplacian eigenfunctions converges to the Liouville measure μ_L rather than only a full-density subsequence? If a full proof is unavailable, what restrictions can be proved on all possible invariant limit measures?
accepted.context_brief: QUE for non-arithmetic negatively curved manifolds

evidence.quote: Rudnick and Sarnak have conjectured that exceptional sequences cannot exist on negatively curved manifolds [27] (that is, the full sequence (µ k)k∈N converges to µ L), this property being called “Quantum Unique Ergodicity” (QUE).
The QUE conjecture is still wide open for non-arithmetic surfaces (and higher-dimensional manifolds).
Rather than proving that all semiclassical measures converge to µ L, one can at least try to obtain some information on the possible limit measures.

accepted.question_text: For eigenfunctions on manifolds of constant negative curvature, can entropy lower bounds for possible semiclassical limit measures be strengthened from at least one half of maximal Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy to maximal entropy, thereby proving Quantum Unique Ergodicity by ruling out partially localized limit measures?

evidence.quote: Recently, some constraints were obtained in the form of non-trivial lower bounds for the Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy of the limit measures [1]: in the case of constant negative curvature, the entropy must be at least half its maximal value, showing that the eigenstates are “at least half-delocalized” (to prove QUE along these lines one would need to remove the half from the lower bound).

accepted.question_text: Can Quantum Unique Ergodicity be disproved by constructing a negatively curved manifold and a sequence of exceptional high-energy eigenstates of the Laplacian, or of a lower-order perturbation of the Laplacian, whose semiclassical measures do not converge to Liouville measure? More generally, does QUE hold only for generic negatively curved surfaces or generic lower-order perturbations rather than for every negatively curved system?
accepted.context_brief: Exceptional eigenstates and genericity of QUE

evidence.quote: On the other hand, disproving QUE amounts to exhibiting a negatively curved manifold and a sequence of exceptional eigenstates of the Laplacian, or of some perturbation of it by lower-order terms.
Like the BGS conjecture, it is possible that QUE holds only for “generic” negatively curved surfaces, or “generic” perturbations of the Laplacian.

accepted.question_text: How much classical chaos is required for Quantum Unique Ergodicity: must the classical dynamics be uniformly hyperbolic, or Anosov, as in geodesic flows on negatively curved manifolds, or can systems with flat parts support exceptional eigenstates such as bouncing-ball modes?
accepted.context_brief: Amount of chaos needed for QUE

evidence.quote: Finally, one may wonder how chaotic a system should be to satisfy QUE.
Does it need to be uniformly hyperbolic (Anosov), like geodesic flows in negative curvature?
Would it be easier to construct exceptional states in case the manifold has some “flat parts”?
The latter question is related with the possible existence of bouncing ball modes in the stadium billiard (which have been clearly identified in numerics) or on similar manifolds [9].

accepted.question_text: Can the random-wave or random-state conjecture for chaotic eigenfunctions be made into a rigorous theorem at microscopic scales, or at intermediate scales between macroscopic size and the wavelength λ^−1? The question asks whether high-energy eigenfunctions ψ_k(x) of chaotic quantum systems have the same statistics as an appropriate random-state ensemble, including value distributions, wavelength-scale correlation functions, nodal sets, and nodal components.

evidence.quote: One would also wish to analyze the wavefunctions ψ k(x) at microscopic scales, or at least some intermediate scale between 1 and the wavelength λ −1.

The main conjecture concerning these microscopic properties is analogous to the BGS conjecture: the eigenfunctions are expected to be statistically equivalent with “random states” in some appropriate ensemble.

The statistical observables to be compared with the random models are manifold. They include the value distribution for {ψ k(x), x ∈ X}, correlation functions at distances ∼ λ −1, the structure of the nodal set {x |ψ k(x) = 0 } and of the complementary nodal components.

To my knowledge, this field of research has mostly consisted in analyzing the properties of the random models, and then numerically checking that these properties are (approximately) satisfied by the eigenstates of some selected quantized chaotic systems.

accepted.question_text: For generic negatively curved surfaces, can one prove L^p-norm and sup-norm bounds for high-energy eigenfunctions that are as small as the norms predicted by random-state models? Current general bounds apply to any Riemannian surface and improve only by negative powers of log λ in negative curvature, while the expected random-state norms are much smaller.
accepted.context_brief: Analytic eigenfunction norm bounds versus random states

evidence.quote: Certain global quantities, like the moments of the distribution {ψ k(x), x ∈ X} (that is the Lp norms ∥ψ k∥p) have also been investigated analytically.
one can obtained upper bounds valid for any Riemannian surface [34], which are usually improved by some negative power of log λ in the negative curvature case.
Still, these upper bounds are expected to be much larger than the Lp norms of “random states”, which are expected to be valid for “generic” negatively curved surfaces.

accepted.question_text: In open quantum chaos for chaotic scattering systems with a fractal trapped set K, resonances λ_k of the meromorphically continued resolvent, and metastable states ψ_k or deformed L^2 eigenstates ψ̃_k, what is the precise connection between the high-energy distribution of resonances and metastable eigenstates on one hand and the chaotic dynamics on K on the other?
accepted.context_brief: Resonances, metastable states, and trapped-set dynamics

evidence.quote: a fractal trapped set K ⊂ S∗X, consisting of points remaining in the (compact) “interaction region” at all times.
each pole λ k of the continued resolvent is a resonance, associated with a metastable state ψ k, which decays with a half-time ∝ 1/ |Imλ k|.
What is the connection between the distribution of high-energy resonances and the eigenstates ψ̃ k on one side, the chaotic dynamics on the trapped set K on the other side?

accepted.question_text: For open chaotic scattering systems, can one prove the fractal Weyl law N(λ,C) ∼ f(C) λ^ν as λ → ∞ for the number of resonances in the strip |Re λ_k| ≤ λ and Im λ_k ≥ −C, where ν = (1 + dim(K))/2 is determined by the Minkowski dimension of the trapped set K and f(C) depends on the strip width? At present, only an upper bound is known for such nonselfadjoint resonance spectra.
accepted.context_brief: Fractal Weyl law for resonance counting

evidence.quote: One expects a fractal Weyl law (2) N(λ,C ) ∼ f (C)λ ν, λ → ∞, where the fractal exponent ν = 1+dim(K) / 2 is related with the (Minkowski) dimension of the trapped set, and f (C) is some function of the strip width.
Yet, the spectra of nonselfadjoint operators are notoriously more difficult to analyze than their selfadjoint counterparts, which explains why only the upper bound in (2) could be proved [33].

accepted.question_text: What is the correct strip-width shape function f(C) in the fractal Weyl law for open quantum chaotic resonance spectra, and how can the fractal exponent ν be reliably checked in real scattering systems rather than only in simplified quantum-map models?
accepted.context_brief: Shape function and exponent in fractal Weyl laws

evidence.quote: An Ansatz for the “shape function” f (C) in (2) was proposed by Schomerus and Tworzydło, in terms of an ensemble of (subunitary) random matrices [29]; so far, the numerical data performed on quantum maps are not very conclusive.
Even numerically checking the exponent ν is a nontrivial task when one deals with a real scattering system [20].

accepted.question_text: For which scattering systems, or for which quantizations of a given open chaotic scattering system, is the fractal Weyl law N(λ,C) ∼ f(C) λ^ν actually valid? The question is whether the law requires a genericity condition, since even the open quantum baker’s map can have parameter choices where the resonance spectrum degenerates to a much smaller density.

evidence.quote: The only system for an asymptotic of the form of (2) could be proved is a simplistic “open quantum baker’s map” [24].
Even in that model, the resonance spectrum may, for some choices of parameters, degenerate to a much smaller density (equivalent with the case of a single periodic geodesic).
This shows that the estimate (2) is probably only true for “generic” scattering systems, or “generic quantizations” of them.

accepted.question_text: Can the fine, for example microscopic, distribution statistics of open quantum chaotic resonance spectra be analyzed beyond the coarse fractal Weyl counting law? This asks for resonance-spacing or local-distribution information in a setting where even the validity of the appropriate Weyl law remains difficult.
accepted.context_brief: Microscopic resonance statistics in open quantum chaos

evidence.quote: Considering the difficulty of settling the validity of this “Weyl law”, analyzing the finer (e.g. “microscopic”) distribution properties of the resonance spectrum seems presently quite difficult.

accepted.question_text: What semiclassical phase-space limit measures can arise from metastable states associated with open quantum chaotic resonances, after restricting attention to the physically relevant interaction region or to deformed L^2 eigenstates? Specifically, does quantum mechanics select a preferred limit measure for these metastable states, or is there a “democracy” in which many semiclassical phase-space distributions can occur?

evidence.quote: The structure of µ k in that region is intimately connected with the classical trapped set K: any limit measure µ of some subsequence (µ kj ) is supported on the unstable manifold of the trapped set; µ is not invariant through the geodesic flow, but decays at the rate Λ = − 2 limk Imλ kj.

As opposed to the case of compact manifolds (where the Liouville measure prevails as a “limit semiclassical measure”), in the present case quantum mechanics does not seem to “preferably select” any limit measure.

Some numerical (and analytical) results in the framework of “open quantum maps” seem to rather indicate a “democracy”, with a multiplicity of semiclassical phase space distributions [16], but the general situation is still unclear at the moment.

evidence.quote: The first question one can ask is “Do we have exact, or at least asymptotic formulas to describe the high-energy eigenvalues/eigenfunctions?” For chaotic systems, and as opposed to the case of completely integrable systems, the answer is “No”.
